title: The and a: o, a, um, uma
description: Say the and a with the right gender, and know when Portuguese leaves the article out.

guide.summary: Every Portuguese noun is masculine or feminine, and the words for the and a show which. Learn o and a, um and uma, the endings that usually tell the gender, the exceptions, and two places where Portuguese and English use articles differently.

sections.title: The and a: o, a, um, uma
sections.text: Portuguese has two words for the and two for a. Masculine nouns take o and um; feminine nouns take a and uma. Adjectives describing the noun follow the same gender.
steps: Find the noun the article belongs to.
Decide masculine or feminine.
For the take o or a; for a take um or uma.

examples.pt: Eu tenho um gato e uma cadeira nova.
examples.en: I have a cat and a new chair.

watch: The word a is both the feminine the and the preposition to; context tells them apart.
Em plus o or a joins into no or na: no carro, na mesa.

sections.title: The ending usually tells you: -o or -a
sections.text: Most nouns ending in -o are masculine and most ending in -a are feminine. For people, the ending follows the person: o irmão, a irmã; o amigo, a amiga.

rows: o carro, o livro, o quarto
a casa, a mesa, a bolsa

steps: Look at the last letter of the noun.
If it is -o, start from masculine; if -a, from feminine.
Check the noun is not one of the exceptions.
watch: The adjective changes with the noun: o carro caro, a bolsa cara.

sections.title: Always feminine: -ção, -dade, -agem
sections.text: Three common endings are reliably feminine, even though -dade and -agem do not end in -a.

rows: a estação, a informação, a lição
a cidade, a universidade, a idade
a viagem, a garagem, a mensagem

steps: Check whether the noun ends in -ção, -dade or -agem.
If it does, it is feminine: a or uma.

examples.en: I am going to take a trip.

watch: Viagem, garagem and mensagem are feminine, even though they do not end in -a. If you know French, beware: le voyage, le garage and le message are masculine there.

sections.title: Exceptions to learn by heart
sections.text: A few everyday nouns break the -o / -a rule. Many words in -ma from Greek are masculine, and foto is feminine because it is short for a fotografia.
steps: Before trusting the ending, check the noun against this list.
Learn each exception with its article, as one unit: o dia, a mão.
Make adjectives agree with the real gender: um dia bonito, uma foto bonita.
watch: Bom dia says it: bom is masculine because dia is.
Mão sounds like irmão but is feminine.

sections.title: Nouns in -e: learn them with the article
sections.text: A noun ending in -e can be either gender, and nothing in the word tells you. Always learn it with o or a.
steps: If the noun ends in -e, do not guess from the ending.
Recall it with its article, as you learned it.
An adjective in -o or -a nearby can confirm the gender.
watch: Adjectives in -e, like quente and grande, have one form for both genders and give no clue.

sections.title: No article for a job after ser
sections.text: English says she is a doctor; Portuguese says Ela é médica, with no article. The article comes back only when you add a description: Ela é uma médica muito boa.
steps: Is the sentence saying what someone does for a living, with ser?
If so, put the job straight after é, with no um or uma.
Make the job match the person: médico, médica.
watch: Ela é a médica means she is the doctor, a particular one.
The same goes for nationality and religion: Ele é brasileiro.

sections.title: O João, a Ana: an article before names
sections.text: In much of Brazil people say o João and a Ana, especially for people they know; in other regions and in formal writing the name stands alone. Both are correct.
steps: Decide whether to use an article; either is fine.
If you use one, take o for a man and a for a woman.
watch: Never um or uma before the name of someone you know.
With an article, em and de join it: Falei com a Ana, a casa da Ana.

steps: Find the noun the article belongs to.
Decide its gender.
Use o for masculine, a for feminine.
Find the noun after the gap.
Decide its gender.
Use um for masculine, uma for feminine.
Look at the last letter of the noun.
Take -o as masculine and -a as feminine.
Make the article and any adjective agree.
Check for the endings -ção, -dade or -agem.
Treat the noun as feminine.
Use a or uma and a feminine adjective.
Check the noun against the exception list.
Use its real gender, not the one the ending suggests.
Make adjectives agree with that gender.
Notice the noun ends in -e.
Recall the article you learned with it.
Use a nearby adjective in -o or -a to confirm.
Check that ser introduces a job.
Leave out um or uma.
Match the job to the person.
Remember the article before a name is optional.
If you use one, match the person: o or a.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for the.
exercises.feedback: The article follows the gender of the noun, and casa is feminine.
exercises.explanation: Casa is feminine (a casa), so the house is a casa.

mistakes.why: O goes with masculine nouns. Casa ends in -a and is feminine, so the masculine article clashes with it.

exercises.instruction: Write the Portuguese word for the.
exercises.feedback: Look at the noun right after the gap, not at mesa.
exercises.explanation: Livro is masculine (o livro), so the book is o livro. The na before mesa already holds the feminine a for the table.

mistakes.why: A is the feminine article. Livro ends in -o and is masculine; mesa is a different noun with its own article.
Um means a, not the. The sentence talks about one particular book.

exercises.instruction: Translate into Portuguese.
exercises.feedback: Check the article and the adjective: both follow carro.
exercises.explanation: Carro is masculine, so the car is o carro, and new takes its masculine form too: novo.

mistakes.why: The feminine article cannot go with carro, a masculine noun ending in -o.
The adjective must agree with carro too, and carro is masculine.
Um means a; the English says the car.

exercises.instruction: Fix the error.
exercises.feedback: The adjective aberta is already right; only one word is wrong.
exercises.explanation: Porta is feminine (a porta), so the door is a porta, which also matches aberta.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. The article in front of porta is masculine, but porta is feminine.
Changing the adjective makes it agree with the wrong article. Porta is feminine, so the article has to change instead.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: The boy opens the window. Leave one tile unused.
exercises.feedback: Each noun takes its own article.
exercises.explanation: Menino is masculine (o menino) and janela is feminine (a janela).

mistakes.why: Janela is feminine, so the masculine article cannot sit before it. The unused tile is the one that does not match janela.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for a.
exercises.feedback: Um and uma follow the noun, just like o and a.
exercises.explanation: Gato is masculine (o gato), so a cat is um gato.

mistakes.why: Uma is for feminine nouns. Gato ends in -o and is masculine.
O means the. The English idea is a cat, one of many.

exercises.instruction: Write the Portuguese word for a.
exercises.hint: Cadeira is feminine; nova agrees with it.
exercises.feedback: The adjective nova already shows the gender.
exercises.explanation: Cadeira is feminine (a cadeira), so a chair is uma cadeira.

mistakes.why: Um is for masculine nouns, and cadeira ends in -a; nova is feminine too.
A means the, but the gap asks for a, any chair.

exercises.instruction: Translate into Portuguese.
exercises.feedback: Check the word for a.
exercises.explanation: Café is masculine, so a coffee is um café. Dropping eu is natural because quero already shows the person.

mistakes.why: Café ends in an accented vowel but it is masculine (o café), so the feminine article does not fit.
That says the coffee, a particular one; the English asks for a coffee.

exercises.instruction: Change the into a. Write the whole sentence.
exercises.hint: O becomes the masculine word for a.
exercises.feedback: The gender stays; only definite becomes indefinite.
exercises.explanation: Cachorro is masculine, so o cachorro becomes um cachorro.

mistakes.why: The gender of cachorro did not change: it is still masculine, so the feminine word for a is wrong.
That is the original sentence: the article was not changed.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: There is a table in the kitchen. Leave one tile unused.
exercises.source: There is a table in the kitchen.

alternatives.message: Also right. Há is the written, more formal way to say there is; in speech Brazilians say tem.

exercises.hint: In Brazil there is is usually tem. Mesa ends in -a.
exercises.feedback: Pick the word for a that matches mesa.
exercises.explanation: Mesa is feminine (a mesa), so a table is uma mesa. Na is em plus a: in the kitchen.

mistakes.why: That tile is the masculine word for a, and mesa is feminine.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for a.
exercises.hint: Look at the last letter of bolsa.
exercises.feedback: Most nouns ending in -a are feminine.
exercises.explanation: Bolsa ends in -a and is feminine, so a bag is uma bolsa.

mistakes.why: Um goes with masculine nouns, usually ending in -o. Bolsa ends in -a.

exercises.instruction: Write the Portuguese word for a.
exercises.hint: Quarto ends in -o, and so does pequeno.
exercises.feedback: The ending -o points to a masculine noun.
exercises.explanation: Quarto ends in -o and is masculine, so a room is um quarto.

mistakes.why: Uma is for feminine nouns; quarto and pequeno both end in -o, the masculine ending.
O means the; after em it would also join into no. The sentence says a room.

exercises.instruction: Replace carro with bolsa and make the sentence agree. Write the whole sentence.
exercises.hint: Bolsa ends in -a, so the article and the adjective change.
exercises.feedback: When the noun changes gender, the article and the adjective follow it.
exercises.explanation: Bolsa is feminine, so o becomes a and caro becomes cara.

mistakes.why: The article still matches carro. Bolsa ends in -a and is feminine.
The adjective was left masculine; it must agree with bolsa as well.

exercises.instruction: Fix the error.
exercises.feedback: For people, the gender follows the person: irmão and irmã.
exercises.explanation: Irmão (brother) is masculine, so a brother is um irmão. The feminine is uma irmã.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. The feminine article does not fit a brother.
That changes the meaning to a sister. Keep the brother and fix the article.

exercises.instruction: Translate into Portuguese.
exercises.feedback: Both the article and the adjective follow cozinha.
exercises.explanation: Cozinha is feminine, so the kitchen is a cozinha and small is pequena.

mistakes.why: Cozinha ends in -a and is feminine; the masculine article clashes with it.
Small must agree with cozinha, a feminine noun.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for the.
exercises.feedback: Nouns ending in -ção are feminine.
exercises.explanation: Estação ends in -ção, and nouns in -ção are feminine, so the station is a estação.

mistakes.why: Estação ends in -ção, an ending that is always feminine, so the masculine article does not fit.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for a.
exercises.feedback: Nouns ending in -agem are feminine, even though they do not end in -a (French voyage is masculine).
exercises.explanation: Viagem ends in -agem, so it is feminine: uma viagem.

mistakes.why: Viagem ends in -agem, a feminine ending, so the masculine word for a is wrong.

exercises.instruction: Write the Portuguese word for the.
exercises.feedback: Bonita already shows the gender.
exercises.explanation: Cidade ends in -dade, and nouns in -dade are feminine, so the city is a cidade.

mistakes.why: Cidade ends in -e, but -dade is a feminine ending; bonita agrees with a feminine noun too.

exercises.instruction: Fix the error.
exercises.feedback: Two words must change: the article and the adjective.
exercises.explanation: Garagem is feminine, like every noun in -agem, so the garage is a garagem and empty becomes vazia.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Nouns ending in -agem are feminine.
The article is fixed, but the adjective still has the masculine ending.

exercises.instruction: Change a into the. Write the whole sentence.
exercises.hint: Uma becomes the feminine word for the.
exercises.feedback: Mensagem stays feminine; only the kind of article changes.
exercises.explanation: Mensagem ends in -agem and is feminine, so uma mensagem becomes a mensagem.

mistakes.why: Mensagem ends in -agem and is feminine, so the masculine article is wrong.
That is the original sentence: the article was not changed.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: The information is right. Leave one tile unused.

alternatives.message: Understandable, but for a fact being correct Brazilians say está certa.

exercises.feedback: Pick the article that matches -ção.
exercises.explanation: Nouns ending in -ção are feminine, so the information is a informação, and right is certa.

mistakes.why: That tile is the masculine article, and nouns ending in -ção are feminine.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for the.
exercises.hint: Problema ends in -a, but it is one of the exceptions.
exercises.feedback: Many words ending in -ma come from Greek and are masculine.
exercises.explanation: Problema is masculine despite its -a: o problema.

mistakes.why: Problema ends in -a, but it is masculine, like sistema and tema. The feminine article does not fit.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for a.
exercises.hint: Foto ends in -o, but bonita gives the gender away.
exercises.feedback: Foto is short for fotografia, which is feminine.
exercises.explanation: Foto is feminine because it is short for a fotografia, so a photo is uma foto, with bonita agreeing.

mistakes.why: Foto ends in -o but it is feminine, short for fotografia; bonita shows that too.

exercises.instruction: Write the Portuguese word for the.
exercises.feedback: Mapa ends in -a but it is masculine.
exercises.explanation: Mapa is masculine: o mapa. Learn it with its article.

mistakes.why: Mapa ends in -a but it is masculine, so the feminine article is wrong.

exercises.instruction: Write the Portuguese word for the.
exercises.hint: Mão ends in -o, but it is an exception.
exercises.feedback: Mão is feminine.
exercises.explanation: Mão is feminine despite its -o sound: a mão.

mistakes.why: Mão ends in -ão like irmão, but it is feminine. The masculine article does not fit.
Uma means a. You raise your hand, a specific one, so Portuguese uses the.

exercises.instruction: Fix the error.
exercises.feedback: The adjective novo is already right.
exercises.explanation: Sistema ends in -ma and is masculine: o sistema. Novo agrees with it.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Sistema is masculine despite the -a.
This makes the adjective agree with the wrong gender. Sistema is masculine, so the article changes, not novo.

exercises.instruction: Translate into Portuguese.
exercises.hint: Dia ends in -a, but it is masculine.
exercises.feedback: Check the article and the adjective in front of dia.
exercises.explanation: Dia is masculine: um dia, and the adjective takes the masculine form bonito or lindo.

mistakes.why: Dia ends in -a, but it is masculine (o dia), so the feminine word for a is wrong.
The adjective must agree with dia, which is masculine.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: I have a problem. Leave one tile unused.
exercises.hint: Problema ends in -a, but it is masculine.
exercises.feedback: Do not trust the -a here.
exercises.explanation: Problema is masculine, so a problem is um problema.

mistakes.why: That tile is the feminine word for a, and problema is masculine despite its -a.

exercises.instruction: Replace mapa with foto and change the article to match. Write the whole sentence.
exercises.hint: Both are exceptions: mapa is masculine, foto is feminine.
exercises.feedback: The article follows the new noun.
exercises.explanation: Foto is feminine, so o mapa becomes a foto.

mistakes.why: The article still matches mapa. Foto ends in -o but is feminine.
That is the original sentence: mapa was not replaced.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for the.
exercises.hint: Leite ends in -e: you have to know it.
exercises.feedback: The -e ending gives no clue; quente does not help either.
exercises.explanation: Leite is masculine: o leite. Nouns in -e must be learned with their article.

mistakes.why: Leite ends in -e, which can be either gender, and this one is masculine.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for the.
exercises.hint: Fria shows the gender of noite.
exercises.feedback: Noite ends in -e, but the adjective has a feminine ending.
exercises.explanation: Noite is feminine: a noite, and fria agrees with it.

mistakes.why: Noite ends in -e, but it is feminine; fria agrees with a feminine noun.

exercises.instruction: Write the Portuguese word for the.
exercises.feedback: Chave ends in -e, so you need to remember it.
exercises.explanation: Chave is feminine: a chave.

mistakes.why: Chave ends in -e, but it is feminine. Learn it as a chave.
Uma means a; the question asks for one particular key.

exercises.instruction: Write the Portuguese word for the.
exercises.feedback: Nome ends in -e, so the article must be learned with it.
exercises.explanation: Nome is masculine: o nome.

mistakes.why: Nome ends in -e, but it is masculine. Learn it as o nome.

exercises.instruction: Replace café with carne and change the article to match. Write the whole sentence.
exercises.feedback: Quente ends in -e and does not change; only the article does.
exercises.explanation: Carne is feminine: a carne. Quente has one form for both genders.

mistakes.why: The article still matches café. Carne is feminine.
Quente has the same form for both genders; there is no quenta.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: The milk is cold. Leave one tile unused.
exercises.feedback: The article and frio must both match leite.
exercises.explanation: Leite is masculine: o leite, and cold takes the masculine form frio.

mistakes.why: That tile is the feminine article, and leite is masculine.

exercises.instruction: Choose the natural way to finish: She is a doctor.
exercises.hint: After ser, a job usually stands alone.
exercises.feedback: English says a doctor; Portuguese drops the article.
exercises.explanation: With ser, a job or profession takes no article: Ela é médica.

mistakes.why: Portuguese leaves out the article before a bare job after ser. The article returns only when a description is added after the job.
That means she is the doctor, a particular one, not what her job is.

exercises.instruction: Write the missing word: he is a teacher.
exercises.source: Meu pai ensina numa escola. Ele é ____.
exercises.feedback: After ser the job needs no article.
exercises.explanation: With ser, a profession stands alone: Ele é professor.

mistakes.why: English needs a here, but Portuguese drops the article before a bare profession after ser.
That is the female form; the teacher here is your father.

exercises.instruction: Translate into Portuguese.
exercises.feedback: Check what follows é.
exercises.explanation: After ser, a profession takes no article: é engenheiro. The article before meu is optional in Brazil.

answers: O meu irmão é um engenheiro.
mistakes.why: English uses an here, but Portuguese leaves the article out before a bare job after ser.

exercises.instruction: Fix the sentence so it sounds natural.
exercises.hint: Look at the word after é.
exercises.feedback: It is a job after ser, with nothing added.
exercises.explanation: A profession after ser takes no article in Portuguese: Pedro é dentista.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. The English a was copied into Portuguese.
That says he is the dentist, a particular one, not what he does for a living.

exercises.instruction: Make the sentence about a woman. Write the whole sentence.
exercises.hint: Change the pronoun and the ending of the job.
exercises.feedback: Still no article: only the gender changes.
exercises.explanation: Médico becomes médica for a woman, and the job still stands without an article.

mistakes.why: Making it feminine does not add an article; a bare job after ser has none.
The job must take the feminine ending for a woman.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: She is a nurse. Leave one tile unused.
exercises.hint: One tile is the English a.
exercises.feedback: After ser, a job has no article.
exercises.explanation: With ser, a profession stands alone: Ela é enfermeira.

mistakes.why: That uses the extra tile. Portuguese drops the article before a bare job after ser.

exercises.instruction: Choose the article that fits before the name.
exercises.feedback: Before a name the article is optional, but if you use one it must match the person.
exercises.explanation: Many Brazilians say O João; plain João is right too. If you put an article, it follows the person: o for a man, a for a woman.

mistakes.why: A is for a woman; João is a man.
Um means a; you do not say a João about someone you know.

exercises.instruction: Translate into Portuguese.
answers: A Ana está em casa hoje.
Hoje a Ana está em casa.
exercises.hint: At home is em casa, with no article.
exercises.feedback: Both A Ana and Ana are right in Brazil.
exercises.explanation: The article before a first name is common in Brazil but optional, so A Ana and Ana are both correct. At home is em casa.

answers: O Ana está em casa hoje.
mistakes.why: Ana is a woman, so a masculine article cannot go before her name.

answers: A Ana está na casa hoje.
mistakes.why: At home is em casa, without the article; na casa means in the house, a particular one.

exercises.instruction: Add the article many Brazilians put before a name. Write the whole sentence.
answers: A Maria mora em São Paulo.
exercises.feedback: The article follows the person: a for a woman.
exercises.explanation: Adding the article is the common spoken form in much of Brazil: A Maria mora em São Paulo.

answers: O Maria mora em São Paulo.
mistakes.why: Maria is a woman, so the masculine article does not fit.
That is the original sentence; the task asks you to add the article.

exercises.instruction: Fix the error.
exercises.feedback: Either fix the article or drop it.
exercises.explanation: An article before a name follows the person: o João. Dropping it, João é meu amigo, is also right.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. The feminine article cannot go before a man’s name.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: Maria is my friend. Leave one tile unused.
exercises.feedback: You may use an article before the name or not, but it has to match.
exercises.explanation: Before a woman’s name the article is a; it is optional in Brazil. Friend is amiga for a woman.

mistakes.why: That tile is the masculine article, and Maria is a woman.
